This book is a great guideline on how to plan out your goals, step by step, and actually follow through on them.  This doesn't just apply to the big goals in life, like buying a house, losing weight, or starting a business; this applies to *every* aspect of your life.

If you have a hard time getting motivated, or you just don't know where to begin, this is the book for you.

Each chapter not only provides practical advice on how to complete your goals but also includes hands-on exercises to step you closer and closer to your personal finish line.

The beauty of "The Lifelong Project" is that its principles apply to any project, whether you're creating a computer program, getting a new job, losing weight, planning a vacation, completing a degree, or building a birdhouse. If it's important to you, it deserves your attention, and Mr. Phillips' guidelines provide an easy, step-by-step process for completion.   Stay is a nice fantasy read. C.C. Jackson did an excellent job of setting the scenes for her story. When she described the underground fey world., I was all but transported there. I could almost smell the earth, feel the the moisture of the dank walls,  feel the rush of the air as Callie learn to fly.
  I love strong female characters. When Callie first learns about her secret heritage, she is hesitant to stay and learn to fight for what is rightfully hers. But as she becomes accustomed to the idea of being a fairy and retaking the throne,  Callie learns she has strengths she never imagined. Following her on the journey was interesting. Does she have what it takes?
  Now...there were a few thing about the book that slightly bothered me. For starters,the relationships between Callie and the two men she becomes involved with felt a little rushed. Callie seems to fall in love every time she is kissed. To be fair, she is supposed to have a special, life-long bond with one of the men, even though she has not seen him in many years. It has been a long time since I was a teenager. Maybe this is just the long-married cynic in me rearing it's jealous little head. This is a fantasy after all!
  Another problem was that the Callie's training and confrontation with the Queen felt a little rushed. The buildup of the story was nice, but I  felt that those sections of the story could have been expanded on. What came after the confrontation could have been much longer. Part of a sequel even.
  I want to say that I did truly enjoy Stay. The things I liked about the book outweigh what I didn't by far. I hope a sequel is written so we can read the further adventures of Callie. Stay is a fun fantasy read and I encourage you to try it for yourself.

"Stay (A Callie Rose Novel)" by C.C. Jackson caught my attention on the first page, when Callie is taken from her home by a dark stranger in the dead of night. Soon after, Callie learns that she is the rightful queen of the Fae in the underground world of Patrona. She faces danger, heartache, and an interesting love triangle as she struggles to become who she was born to be.

This book was a fun read and I recommend it to YA readers who enjoy entertaining, romantic tales about the magical world of faeries. It is a quick read, (perhaps just a bit rushed--sometimes the dialogue felt a little "off" and there were some spelling and gramatical errors), but overall, a light, engaging and delightful story.

I look forward to your second book, Ms. Jackson!

Stay by C.C. Jackson follows a girl, Callie Rose, ripped from her home in the middle of the night and forced into the world of the fae-a world she once belonged to, but has long since forgotten.

I bought this book because it was only 99 cents and came highly recommended by a couple friends. While the dialogue came off as a little too formal in my opinion (after all, this is a young adult book), Stay was fast-paced and a truly quick read-I finished it in two hours.

I absolutely cannot stand weak heroines who rely on others to guide them through their life journey. Callie was definitely not one of those people. While she came off as a little whiny sometimes, she certainly stepped up her game by the end of the book and took charge of the situation. She initially tried to avoid her responsibilities but, eventually, Callie came to realize the necessity of her actions and she literally fought for what she wanted and so what she thought was right.

The romance, or rather, the love triangle, was also a little rushed and both of the "potential guys" seemed bipolar and weird. But in the end, I approved of Callie's decision with regards to who she should be with.

Overall, I recommend this book to anyone with a love of faeries and who are just in need of a quick, and relatively good, read.

I thoroughly enjoyed this book, and shared it with an avid-reader friend of mine, who dubbed it "a good sizzler!" It's exactly that! It is hopping and jumping with action, and humor as well. It's hard to pull off that combination; if the humor isn't done right in a book with an otherwise dark tone, it falls flat, or takes away from the seriousness of the plotline. Here, weighty issues of morality and politics are the main fare, not to mention tense suspense, but at points I found myself laughing out loud. Shane Fetters, the antagonist, is a buffoon; we have to take him seriously, because he's a dangerous buffoon, but the scene where he crashes an important lunch hosted by his father, wearing stolen sunglasses to hide his bar-brawl black eye, is one of the funniest in the book. Jack McEnroe, the hero, isn't perfect but he's tough and likable; he's one of the good guys, although flawed, kind of like many of Stephen King's main characters. Even secondary characters are nuanced, such as Jack's ex-wife, and the elder Fetters, the head of the contracting company charged with building the super-maximum-security prison. Set aside a block of time for this -- you will not want to put it down.

Keir Graff delivers again in this fast paced, dark thriller. Jack McEnroe is an exciting mix of stoic and crazy that makes you root for him, but also wonder about his secrets. Shane Fetters is a Fargo-esque bad guy whose unraveling draws you in from the start. He's part doofus and part sociopath. You can see the demented hamster wheel turning in his head. Graff brought a vibrance to this novel that makes it great. He goes beyond typical crime novels and shows an aptitude for literary greatness.  The scenes and characters are memorable and left me wanting more.

reviewText:
Keir Graff's latest book is an engrossing, fast-paced read, with two characteristics that particularly appealed to me for two reasons.

First, Graff is a master at characterization.  I found myself picturing the main characters very clearly, although there was no point where he described them at length. Also, the characters are multi-dimensional. The good guys (and women) have some serious flaws, and with an exception or two, the bad guys have some redeeming qualities.  I plan to reread the book at some point simply to trace how Graff developed his characters so subtly, yet so effectively.

Secondly, the story is an accurate reflection of the contemporary American West, where I have spent most of my adult life. Graff's book touches on several of the themes that affect life here, particularly the desperation of rural areas to attract industries and projects that will provide jobs in a land where natural resource extraction no longer supports the economy,and the social tensions and envies that arise when wealthy newcomers establish a lifestyle that long-time residents cannot afford. Graff also employs humor that shows he knows he way around the West.  I laughed aloud when an impatient out-of-towner waiting for her luggage in a small airport comments that the ticket seller must also be the person who unloads baggage; anyone who flies around this part of the country knows that is often true.

I thoroughly enjoyed this book and now I intend to read Graff's earlier works.

I have read and LOVED all four novels from the incredibly talented Keir Graff. I also found that, after finishing each one, I was left wanting more and couldn't wait for the next adventure to be unleashed! So, I highly recommend you order your copy of The Price of Liberty, strap yourself in and enjoy the ride!

Keir Graff is a talented `new-to-me' writer and I'm very excited about reading the balance of his work.

Readers will notice from page one that Graff has a masterful ear for dialogue, what makes a good line in fiction and what really rings true from a character's viewpoint. In short it seems Graff is a master of characterization. As I read this book I kept laughing and saying to myself "I know these people"...

Set in Wyoming, I had the pleasure and pain of growing up out West; Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, and Utah. I have to say that Graff nailed the sensibility of folks in these parts. He also feels a great deal for his characters because if they were written with less nuance and smartness (even the dumb ones) they simply would become cliches...

But that doesn't even come close to happening in TPoL. What I felt (and perhaps I'm dating myself here) was akin to reading the vivid characters and story telling on a par with early James Crumley novels (like Last Good Kiss) and Edward Abbey novels (like Desert Solitaire, although the plot contains a modicum less anarchy than an Abbey novel).

Prickly, fleshed out, humorous and smart. All are the folks you will find inhabit the world of Red Rock, Wyoming where the story is set. I will say that I'm not super current the action genre (not typically reading books where bodies pile up like matchsticks) but Graff's writing could get me over there - just as Crumley and Abby's novels have done in the past. Enjoyable, high quality, page turners...

TPoL is straightforward story of deceit and greed populated, again, by real seeming characters. The book also offers an interesting dichotomy of the American popular male/female ethos...

The hero, Jack McEnroe (great name BTW) is a moral relativist (aren't we all?) who acts out his emotional range with honor and his physical body. Punch first, think later. Where-as the women in the novel, like Jack's ex-wife and mother to his kids, Jack's hipster girlfriend wanna-be, and old, personal friend, the revered and feared local librarian, are all women that carry with them the better virtues that comes with thought before action. They are the moral compass of the action in the book.

And there is lots of action too! In this world we also see that two of the worse actors (the father and son team of villains who of course end up paying the price of liberty), that it turns out these are men completely cut off from women and any of their good and moderating influences (they live in a giant man-cave for gosh sakes!)...

So without women where would we be? Would it be just life and death world of the modern American Wild West??? Certainly seems so in TPoL...

But don't let my literary deconstruction, valid or not, get in the way of your buying this book for a purely entertaining read...It's just that the writing is so darn good it begs the question to look more deeply and see what Keir Graff is saying about sex and culture in this day and age.

Buy his book and become a big fan.
summary: Buy this book and become a big fan

reviewText:
This is my third Keir Graff novel (4th if you include his first, Cold Lessons [also great!], which was written under the pseudonym Michael McCulloch) and my conclusion is that Graff is one of the very best in the political/thriller genre.  This novel is fast reading and VERY entertaining. 2 words: Page turner.

My only regret after finishing The Price of Liberty is that I have to wait for him to write his next book!  Read it!

Keir Graff has shown himself to be a fine writer since his first book, but he kicks his talent into overdrive with The Price of Liberty, a thinking person's thriller that pits one decent man against forces out to cynically profit from overblown fears of terrorist threats. Graff takes on profiteering military contractors in the same sly, entertaining and righteous fashion that Carl Hiaasen demolishes corrupt developers who happily pave over fragile ecosystems for a buck. This is a page-turner full of colorful characters, snappy dialogue, bracing humor and believable twists you won't see coming until they jump off the page and grab you. One of the year's best.

In the 1970s one of the foremost writers of action packed heroic fantasy  was Lin Carter. This book collects the first two volumes of what was  perhaps Carter's best series. The Jandar of Callisto books were written  very much in the tradition of the John Carter of Mars novels by Edgar Rice  Burroughs, but without Burroughs' semi victorian language. I read the  Callisto books when I was a kid and still find them to be a lot of fun.  This book is full of pageantry, romance and swordplay. Callisto, or  Thanator as the natives call it, is a wondrous world of flying ships and  dense jungles teeming with danger. Anyone who enjoys a fast paced adventure  story set on an exotic alien world should definitely give Callisto a try.  In addition to his writing, Lin Carter was one of the most influential  editors of fantasy fiction. He is remembered today primarily for getting  many classics of the genre back into print. But Carter could spin a  wonderful yarn, and it's great to see his work available again for new  readers to discover.
summary: The return of a fantasy great.

reviewText:
I was really excited about this book when I first started reading it.  I thought it would finally be the kind of book that restored literary merit to the romance genre.  The protagonist was interesting and unusual and most importantly, physically imperfect like the rest of us.  She was also a middle aged woman rather than your ordinary, beautiful 20-something heroine. I loved how the author switched between the 2 story-tellers of the sisters, too. And at first, it proved to be a story that I enjoyed.

But about halfway into the book, I realized that this story was taking its fresh ideas and turning them into the same old paperback crap romance stories always turn out to be.  Put simply, it tried to go on too long.  And, as if stuck for ideas or having tired of the story, the author began to depend on those conventions typical stories do: now they're together, Ooh, now they're not, Oh! Together again! Uhm... surprise??  Cant really go on about all the
Other plot points I found disappointing and unimaginative because it might spoil it for you.

Because the first half of the book was so enjoyable and well-written, I've given this a 3.  Otherwise, purely because of plot defects and stringing the book along til the author beat the last gasp of enjoyment out of the book, I'd of given it a 1.

reviewText: One of my favorite books and the best I have read this year. It is said that love is blind but Linda Gillard has written a story that allows the reader to see love through eyes that are amazingly clear.  As mysterious Keir describes everyday objects to blind Marianne, she finds her heart that had been frozen by unbelievable tragedy is responding to his words.  Her sister, Lou, and Garth the Goth add some comic relief and emotional support. This is a beautiful, not-to-be-missed love story.

Star Gazing is a heartwarming story unlike no other I have read before.  The characters are very real, flaws and all.  I loved the way the sense of smell, hearing and touch come into play in this book as the story progresses.  Nice twist of plot as well.  If you want a romance that is not formulaic, but entertaining, you will love Star Gazing.

This book was a recommended read for my reading group.  I thoroughly enjoyed it.  While at heart a romance, STAR GAZING also deals with blindness and how one blind woman relates to the world in a sensitive and thought-provoking way.  There is also a strong environmental message.

I first heard about STAR GAZING through Valerie's lovely review over at Life is a Patchwork Quilt. And I have to thank her for that review because I don't think I would otherwise have come across Linda Gillard's work. Gillard is a Scottish author who lived for several years on the Isle of Skye, where much of this book takes place. From what I can tell, her books tend to focus on women above the age of 35, who are dealing with the everyday, yet perilous issues of adulthood, aging, love, mental health, family, etc. As such, they sounded sort of awesome to me, and I immediately placed her most recent book on my wishlist. It seemed unique and appealed to me for several reasons, including the fact that the main character is a blind widow. The setting was also a draw. I have only been to Scotland once, but it made a lasting impression on me and I love reading books set there. So that's why I was so excited to receive a copy of STAR GAZING for my birthday. I cracked it open that night, fell in love immediately, and pretty much flew through it. Marianne Fraser has several valid reasons to be as angry as she is. Blind since birth, she's navigated her way through life without the ability to see what's coming at her. Widowed just a few years into her marriage, her grief was compounded by the fact that she was pregnant at the time and lost the baby shortly after the horrible accident that took her husband Harvey. Living with her sister Louisa in a flat neither of them much like, she goes about her daily routine with almost furious precision. Counting and memorizing the number of steps from here to there, she has a place for everything. Her few outlets include walking through the park, touching the trees, listening to the rain, and going to the occasional opera. One snowy eve she drops her key outside her door and a man comes along and offers to help her find it. Not thinking much of it at the time, she finds herself remembering his voice at odd times. So that when she randomly comes across him again on her next opera outing, Marianne is surprised at how pleased she is to have a chance to talk with him again. Keir Harvey shares more than just his last name with her departed husband, though. He, too, works on an oil rig, predicting where the best places to drill are, how complications will arise, and when storms might interfere with the work. Originally from the Isle of Sky, he returns home as often as he can to the only place he feels truly comfortable. When he offers to take Marianne there and show her the beauty of that wild place, she throws her habitual caution to the winds and jumps at the chance. I ended this book so conflicted! The first half is literally moving. Simply and carefully written, it is so beautiful and readable. I was almost instantly enamored of Marianne and the dogged way she went about living what was left of her life. Even though I could not perfectly understand the monumental challenges she faced on a constant basis, I felt as though I was there right there with her. Her frustration and longing were palpable to me and I allowed myself to hope just a little bit along with her that Keir would be the unlooked for sweet resolution to her years of struggle and pain. Keir is a wonderful character. Strong and extremely blunt in his speech and mannerisms, he pushes Marianne to move past her carefully constructed inhibitions, even as he carves out a space of peace and gentleness for her in his life. Their interactions are taut and quietly affecting. Marianne's sister Louisa and her hilarious assistant Garth the Goth brought a nice level of humor and warmth to the story and I found myself laughing more than once at this homey woman who writes vampire romance novels by the score, takes care of her sister, and finds herself in the most unexpected of romantic scenarios. Suffice it to say, I was hooked. And then somewhere along the way things got murky. Marianne's anger and fears overwhelmed her and things got out of step between all of them. That in and of itself did not bother me at all. Rather it moved the tale forward in interesting and complex ways. But it never seemed to find its rhythm again after that. The conflict grew and grew and their interactions became stilted to the point that I was crying out for some sort of harkening back to that original connection they formed to relieve the awkwardness that had taken over. Somewhere along the way my involvement was severed and by the time the ending arrived I had become lost and could not find my way back to that breathless place of discovery that so enchanted me for the half of the novel. I guess I wanted a little more time to explore the resolution they came to. That said, I enjoyed it enough that I am definitely going to seek out Ms. Gillard's earlier work. Emotional Geology in particular looks good and I foresee myself ordering it in the very near future as I loved the first part of STAR GAZING.

Star Gazing is one of those rare books I wished would never end.  It is the story of Marianne, blind since birth, widowed young, and childless since she miscarried her baby shortly after her husband's tragic death.  She lives with her beloved older sister who writes what Marianne considers silly novels, and then there is her sister's Goth assistant, a young man in make-up, piercings, and odd clothing.

Enter Keir, a tall man from Skye who has the ability to treat Marianne like a normal person, except that he can describe things using music and language so well that she can "see" them.  He takes her to his home on the Isle of Skye to show her the stars, and does just that.

This love story and the four characters went directly to my heart as I read.  If you've ever known a blind person, you know how difficult it is to describe things to him.  Keir's loving consideration of Marianne's blindness and her crabbiness when her life skills fail her, is enough to make the reader fall in love with him too.

Like any love story, the course of it doesn't run smooth, partly because Marianne fears losing him if she falls in love.  I must stop before I give the whole story away.  Please read this one; it's the best book I've read in a long time.
summary: From the Isle of Skye with Love

reviewText: Star Gazing is one of those books that keeps you up til 4am with its twists and turns, engrossing story and totally yummy hero. I've lent it to many friends since I read it and we've all fallen in love with Keir who takes the blind heroine to the Isle of Skye to "show" her the stars. This book has everything - romance, humour, suspense, scenery and a cast of characters who will stay with you long after you finish it. I laughed out loud and cried my eyes out.

This is the third book of Linda's, all read rather closely together. This isn't a problem, however, as each book is very different. In Star Gazing, Linda brings us Marianne, a 45 year old woman who's been blind since birth, and already a widow. She is fiercely independant, stubborn, and passionate, with a love of nature.

Already in her life is her warm-hearted sister, who has helped her since the death of her husband. The relationship between them is not always easy, as they often disagree.. but the love and support is obvious.

Into her life steps Keir, and once again Linda has written a strong hero. He's not embarressed or thrown by her blindness, but rather tries to explain things to her, by comparing them to music. Whilst be extremely kind and caring, he also allows her to keep that independance.

The most fascinating part of the book for me was Marianne's experience as a blind person, and the way that Linda brings this across. When Keir took her to Skye, I felt as if I could experience it all, but the way that Marianne did. It's wonderfully written.

Linda has become one of my favourite authors, and I am constantly recommending her books to people. This one is a lovely, unique romantic tale, which also deals with issues such as bereavement and blindness.

I loved this book right from the start. The characters are so well drawn and the story so moving. Marianne is very independent, and a little prickly. She doesn't like to use her cane when she's out because she doesn't want it to be obvious she's blind. Some of the things she said made me smile, but you could also really feel her pain, both at the loss of her husband, and the other losses that she suffers.

Linda Gillard's writing seems to have so much feeling to it and I really cared what happened to Marianne and Keir. There's also Louisa and her relationship with the much younger Garth the Goth.

Because the main character is blind, there's a lot of description of Edinburgh and Skye, two wonderful settings. And the things Keir does to be able to describe surroundings to Marianne are very touching.

A lovely book, and one which I highly recommend. A 5/5 for me.
Not my type of book - too predicable.  But it is a good first effort.

Our neighborhood book club chose to read Deborah Wolfe's book because one of our members knew a friend of a friend of the author and, on the whole, I'm glad we did.

The book club members are all ladies of about the same age as the author, many of us have daughters and most of us are continually questioning our childrearing practices.  The discussion about the book really took off quickly and easily.  However, although we all enjoyed it and found it hard to put down once we had got going we felt there were definate flaws in the novel.  The character's of the mother and both daughters were painted in watercolors rather than bold oilpaints, they did not become real enough to deal with the tremendous emotional battles they were forced to wage. I was forced to acknowledge too many times that Ally had a good figure and I lost count of how many hot baths I read about. The story would have had more weight to it if we had more facts about how she dealt with the practical issues of widowhood - money problems, socializing without a partner etc. rather than learning about what clothes she wore on each day.

We found the last scenes in the book incredibly emotional and moving but we were left quite cold by the eldest daughter's struggles as she deals with her changing condition.

Many of the group wanted to give it to teenage daughters to read but I don't think I want to give it to mine - Lydia got off very lightly and seemed to have no lasting wounds from her misfortunes.  I also don't know if I would recommend it to friends who became widows - Ally also came through her traumas remarkably easily.

A four star rating is rather high but then I think back to what an enjoyable meeting we had whilst discussing the book - wine flowed, I got to know more about the women around me and I look forward to tackling our next book club choice.  (There Is No Me Without You by Melissa Fay Green).
summary: Good Books Lead to Good Discussions

I will definitely recommend 'With You and Without You' to friends.

Deborah Wolf's first book is a very descriptive look inside the life of a young family life dealing with the loss of the girls' father.  She adds the details of time and place that make you feel as if you are a houseguest watching the story unfold.  A quick and pleasant summer read.

Ally's husband Patrick was killed in a car accident, leaving her to raise their two daughters Lydia and Becca alone.  Patrick's death is heartbreaking and his absence from their lives is deeply felt.

Ally feels her daughters slowly, but surely pulling away from her.  Eleven year-old Becca is sad and aloof and fourteen year old Lydia is shutting herself off from everyone except her boyfriend Eric.  When another crisis befalls the family, this time from Lydia, Ally is frustrated and angry at both Lydia and herself. She is feeling guilty and helpless as well.

Patrick's best friend Michael is still a fixture in their lives and Ally cherishes his friendship.  Eventually, Ally and Michael's relationship starts to become something more.  Ally wants Michael as her lover but losing him as a friend, if things should not work out is unfathomable for her.  Michael is the one steady thing in her life right now and she simply could not handle losing him.

Ally, Lydia, Becca and Michael have many challenges to face.  The one certainty in their lives, is their love for each other.  That love will be the strength that guides them through the rough road ahead of them.

With you and Without You is a very poignant story.  It is written in the first person from Ally's point of view.  The impact of losing Patrick is devastating for everyone.  Lydia has a life changing experience and Ally faces the daily battle of where she fits in her daughter's plight.  Young Becca keeps the family grounded and Michael plays a huge part in the women's lives.  It's his strength, love, and support that Ally draws her strength from.  Although I may have handled a few things differently than Ally has, I have so much respect and admiration for her and her girls.  With You and Without You is an inspiring story.  It makes you want to appreciate everything and take nothing for granted.  It's wonderful.

Nannette

The Bite Before Christmas by Heidi Betts is fun and sexy anthology that you really can sink your teeth into.

All I Vant For Christmas has Connor Drake just wanting an all out festive holiday season. He can't get his vampire siblings to partake of the holiday cheer so he turns to his friend Angelina Ricci for help.  She recommends event coordinator Jillian Parker to deck the family halls. Will Jillian be able to fulfill her duties for a family of vampires?  And can Connor turn on the Drake charm to get Jillian to share the holidays with him?

Vivian Harrison secret crush on her boss Sean Spicer comes out in the open in A Vampire In Her Stocking. Vivian learns Sean is terminally ill and confides in her friend and fellow vampire Angelina. Angelina decides to give Vivian the ultimate present by turning Sean for her but will Sean embrace his new vampire powers?

It's A Wonderful Bite has matchmaker to the vampires wondering if her life would have been different if she wasn't a vampire. Angelina wakes to find her and her love Ian Hart living life as mortals and its not the glamorous life she is used to living.  Angelina and Ian's relationship grows stronger by the lessons of her dream.

The Bite Before Christmas is spicy, funny and wickedly sexy.  Each couple has different stories to tell and each is a compelling read.  This anthology will keep you warm on those cold winter nights.  It's a delightful read.

This book contains three novellas about vampires and Christmas.  Frankly, I wouldn't have guessed the two could be combined in any form worth reading but Betts has done it.  This is not a literary masterpiece but it is a fun, very sexy (yes, erotic)read.  If you are looking for something vampire light with a holiday feel then this one is for you.

In response to other reviewers: The cover guy is appropriate, he looks just like what I picture Ian to look like (not so much like Connor or Sean).

Also the names of the men in the Kindle edition that I read have been changed. Nick is Sean and Sergio is Ian.

I am surprised...PLEASANTLY. This was really a great book (anthology/novellas) for free. I like how the author intertwined the characters in the story; yet, each was interesting and unique.

If you answered, "Yes!" you'll truly enjoy this group of three delightful stories. Quick moving stories with romance, laughter and fun... all set near the Christmas holidays.  Well-written and all three stories stand alone while having connecting characters. Delightful!
Funny cute stories.  Who knew vampires celebrated Christmas?  Though being undead one wonders the theology.

reviewText:
The first story was good, but I liked the second story better. I read some of the other reviews before I read all three and more than one person knocked the story titled "Vampire in my Stocking", but it's honestly a great little read. I don't see why they were raving about the first one so much and wanting more, I think the entire story ran its course within those pages. Connor and Jillian weren't so great together that I wanted to know more about them, but then again, neither was Sean and Vivian.

It's the third story that threw me for a bit of a loop. Everybody criticized that one, and I have to say it was strange to say the least. Heidi Betts writes well, a little corny at times (her corniness is also apparent in her little bio in the back of the book), but overall a good writer. I just think the fact that she wrote the character Angelina void of any personality simply because she was human was going overboard. Not only did she write Angelina without personality, but she chipped away at her morals and taste as well. According to Betts, vamps are just better than regular people all the way around. In this other reality the human Angelina lived a bit like a vagabond slob for no reason at all and constantly criticized the fact that she had regular hearing and eyesight and strength, but the way she complained sounded like a deep self hatred.

This sounds almost laughable, but does the woman who wrote these stories honestly want to be a vampire? It's one thing to be creative with telling a tale, but she writes as if being human is loathsome, an outright burden of some sort. It's weird almost. I don't know if I'll read anymore of her books, but that last story seemed to tell a tale of its own about the author herself that I'm not sure I wanted to know.
summary: None of them are exactly 5 rate stories...

reviewText:
First off, the title of this book clearly makes this a light read so I'm putting away the long knives. I tried to read this book as a lighthearted romantic story, and it succeeded. I found the three stories All I Vant For Christmas, A Vampire In Her Stocking, and It's A Wonderful Bite to be entertaining. On the hotness scale, this book does have sizzling explicit scenes. But in places I did slap myself in the forehead and did my best Homer Simpson impersonation, "DOH!" I'll share some of my favorites with you.

  "'Holy razor blades, Batman,' she breathed..."

  "...he could feel the dampness between her legs just from where they pressed together like Twinkies inside their cellophane wrapper."

  "She yipped, actually yipped like a puppy with its tail caught in a door."

  "Vivian yipped...actually yipped like some frou-frou pocket Chihuahua...and spun around to find Sean standing in front of the fireplace."

Now to the book, I'm going to break down the book and ask a series of questions and give each section a number rating with the best being 100%.

Opening Scene: 14/15 points

1) Does the opening pull you into the story?
The stories are short and compact. They hook you right from the get go.

2) Is the opening bogged down with back story?
There's not much back story. The stories are crammed together with a vampire matchmaker as the character tying them all together.

3) Does the first scene prompt you to read more?
I think they do their job.

4) Do you have a sense of time and place?
Yes, everything felt right with time and place.

Plot: 10/15 points

5) Is the plot fresh and appealing even if it contains familiar romantic ingredients?
They feel like they were reworks of previously published plots. The It's A Wonderful Life Plot was fine for what it was, but I feel that the stories were too short to develop their own uniqueness.

6) Is the story problem evident?
Yes, the author gets to the crux of the matter quickly.

7) Can you see an initial hint of external conflict in these first pages?
Due to the story format the external conflicts are in the forefront.

8) Is the pacing effective?
It works for this multistory format.

9) Are transitions smooth an easy-to-follow?
I did not have any problems with the transitions.

10) Does the chapter end so you would want to turn the page?
I did not feel the hooks, but I keep turning the pages.

Narrative/Dialogue: 10/20 points

11) Is the narrative compelling with vivid descriptions and pertinent details?
The descriptions were fine, but the inconstantly marked, sometimes parentheses sometimes italics, internal dialogue threw me off.

12) Are the five senses used to enhance the setting/emotions of the characters?
The five sense were used, but some of the similes and metaphors popped me out of the book.

13) Is the setting recognizable?
Yes, the were all very concrete descriptions.

14) Is the narrative intrusive?
I would say it was occasionally intrusive. I could often hear the author's voice.

15) Are narrative and dialogue balanced?
I felt the narrative and dialogue could have used more polish.

16) Is the dialogue natural for the character?
This was a big one for me. In the first story, the Heroine had a quirky, pop reference, voice that I felt reflected her personality. Then the serious Hero started having the pop references, and then it continued through the whole book with each Heroine. I felt it was the author's voice trying to add a little levity to the characters but by doing so removed their unique voices that we only had a short time to get to know.

17) Does each character have a distinctive voice?
No.

18) Does the dialogue move the story forward or is it used as a back story/information dump?
Heidi does a good job with only including the information we need to move the plot along.

19) Is action interspersed with dialogue so that characters aren't "talking heads"?
No talking heads everything moves along quite nicely.

Writing Technique: 10/20 points

20) Is the book presented professionally with few typos and generally accepted punctuation?
I did not find any typos, but the use of parentheses and italics for internal dialogue confused me. Honestly, I kept thinking the parenthetical statements were from the author. Also, the overuse of EM dashes reduced their impact in the sentences where they were most needed. In the first story, there was a few instances of head hopping (page 34 & 48) but the rest of the book seemed fine.

21) Does the author have a unique voice that makes this book stand out?
Yes, but it often interfered with the characters voice.

22) Is the writing easy-to-read with varied sentence length and structure?
Yes, there was good variation.

23) Is action shown, not told?
The action was solid and quick.

24) Is the point of view handled appropriately?
As mentioned, there were a few stumbles in the first story.

25) Are transitions of time and setting logical and smooth?
I did not have any problems with them.

Characterization: 10/15 points

26) Are the hero/heroine introduced in a timely manner or their meeting foreshadowed?
Yes, very quickly.

27) Are the characters well developed with believable strengths and flaws?
The strengths and flaws were clear, but the characters did not have time to develop fully.

28) Is the relationship between the hero/heroine emotional as well as physical?
Oh, yes.

29) Do you believe these characters will achieve happily-ever-after?
All had H.E.A. endings.

30) Are the secondary characters appropriate to the story?
They were fine.

31) Are the heroine's goals/conflicts identifiable?
Yes, they got straight to the point that's for sure.

32) Does her motivation make her actions believable?
Their motivations were fair.

33) Are the hero's goals/conflicts identifiable?
Yep, as I said straight to the point.

34) Does his motivation make his actions believable?
They were all convincing. I would have liked to have seen more depth, but that was not possible in this format.

Romance: 14/15 points

35) Are the romance elements present?
They were sizzling!

So for The Bite Before Christmas I give a total of: 68% or 3.4 stars.

reviewText:
Three Christmas vampire stories
ALL I VANT FOR CHRISTMAS
Connor Drake is a vampire he is a multi-millionaire business man, he owns a chain of successful restaurants. His brother Liam and sister Maeve live with him in his mansion. He would really like to have a traditional Christmas with all the trimmings, but Liam and Maeve, despise his ideas and their relationship is strained. His friend Angelina Ricci who runs a matchmaking business, suggests he hire her friend Jillian Parker an events planner. Jillian is pretty nervous at going to see Connor, vampires are accepted in society nevertheless she is apprehensive. Nothing though could have prepared her for the gorgeous guy who is before her, vampire or not he is one hunk. Conner is bowled over by this beautiful human woman, and plots how to get to know her better, insisting she live in while she decorates his home is definitely the way to go.
A VAMPIRE IN HER STOCKING
Vivian Harrison is a vampire, although her boss Sean Spicer does not know this, Vivian is his personal assistant, where they work at the DNN news network. One evening he calls her into his office to tell her he is leaving, Vivian is devastated she has been in love with Sean for ages, he explains that he has a brain tumour that is inoperable and he is going to die. Vivian loses control and jumps him they end up making hot love accross his desk. Later at home crying she tells her best friend Angelina Ricci all about it, Angelina is a vampire as well. After her friend goes home Vivian goes to bed to try to sleep. When she wakes the next morning it is to find Sean unconscious on her sofa with a big red ribbon with a tag wishing her merry Christsmas from Angelina. She had turned Sean into a vampire.
IT'S A WONDERFUL BITE
Angelina Ricci runs a successful matchmaking business she has lived with her boyfriend Ian Hart for years, he is a cop. Angelina has loved Ian forever and would love to get married, but Ian is a man of few words yep, no or grunts are the most she ever gets from him. Ian is a vampire as well, but he does have his soft side at this time of year he loves watching the old classic "It's a Wonderful Life". After watching the film in bed with Ian, Angelina falls asleep and has a terrible dream where they are both human, Ian is married and she is the other woman. Both of them are cops on a stake-out watching a house full of vamps, then Ian gets captured.
These are three fabulous novellas they are a good length too. Really well written, with great character development and good story lines. Angelina Ricci is the character that connects all the stories, she helps her friends find true love. Highly recommend these three hot stories.

The three books are a good quick read and enjoyable if you like a bit of erotica in your vampire stories.

The first book was my favorite, and I think it should have been a full length novel all it's own.  I was just getting attached to the characters and would loved to have read more interaction with Liam and Maeve.

With the second book, I was pleasantly surprised to see them mentioned briefly and hoped to *see* more of them.

The third story was my least favorite.  It was just a little too 'Ghost of Christmas Past' turned present that just seemed a bit odd and I couldn't really get into it.

ALL I VANT FOR CHRISTMAS:  Connor Drake's deepest holiday wish is an old fashioned Christmas the likes of which he fondly remembers from his humanity, full of family and love. His reluctant and recalcitrant younger brother and sister, however, can hardly be bothered. As a favor for her good friend, vampire matchmaker Angelina Ricci sends him Jillian Parker, a young...and human...event coordinator starting to make a name for herself. Jillian understands intellectually that vampires aren't the bloodthirsty monsters of books and movies, but working for one, being in his house, makes her decidedly nervous...the fact that Connor is gorgeous, intelligent, kind, and gorgeous (it bears repeating), makes her feel something else entirely.

With Jillian, Connor may get a much happier holiday than he'd ever dreamed, but only if the young woman can become comfortable with his vampire nature.

A VAMPIRE IN HER STOCKING:  Vampire Vivian Harrison is heartbroken when her boss Sean Spicer tells her he's dying. She's been in love with him for years. The announcement spurs her into wild waters and before she knows it, she and Sean have shared a single desperate moment of passion. The gaping loss following their time together threatens to crush her, until one evening, an unconscious and bow-wrapped Sean Spicer shows up on her couch, sporting a couple of fang marks on his neck and a new undead status...with a card from best friend Angelina Ricci, matchmaker and meddler, wishing her a Merry Christmas.

He never knew she was a vampire; she had no doubt he didn't want to be one. He may be the best present she's ever received, but Vivian has no illusions that Sean will have any interest in decking her halls when he finds out what's happened to him.

IT'S A WONDERFUL BITE:  Despite the holiday cheer and comfortable life, despite the love of her long time lover Ian, matchmaker Angelina Ricci felt a yearning for more, for the tinsel on the tree, so to speak. As friends around her have found their mates (thanks to her), she feels an odd sort of need to have Ian take their relationship to a new level. But the vampire cop isn't exactly a hearts and romance sort of guy, and he's got no use for human traditions like marriage.

Waking up on Christmas morning is a shock, though, when Angelina realizes that she's stuck in a nightmare. She's human, and so is Ian. They're partners...but not in life. They're cop partners and Ian is married with children - he's someone else's husband, someone else's father. She's his lover on the side. And from all indications, that was her own fault. When their job...and she shudders at the thought...puts Ian's life in the gravest danger at the fangs of a group of rogue vampires, Angelina has to rely on skills limited by her human shell to save them both. Hoping all the while that the horrific nightmare will soon be over.

These three heartwarming and solid novellas are loosely connected through the character of Angelina Ricci, and Heidi Betts has done a good job instilling her romances with holiday warmth and a sensual heat. Betts is deft with character definition and does reasonably well providing three complete, satisfying stories with a limiting length. None are terribly complex in plot, nor are the characters overly complicated, but they don't have to be to be lightly entertaining and romantic.

The second title, "A Vampire in Her Stocking", was my least favorite of the three. I didn't like the beginning and it took me a long time to warm up to Vivian, who I found to be a bit whiney and drippy, and Sean, who I thought was a bit thoughtless in his treatment of Vivian. Still, it was the first title, "All I Vant for Christmas," that I felt was the least complete within its own pages, ending rather abruptly with several questions and plot threads dangling, though there were some very pleasing resolution and wrap up provided in exposition in the final story.

I enjoyed this set of holiday PNR romances. Each story had a very unique flavor and the plots were different enough to provide genuine variety, even with the thread of loose connection through them all. Overall, I found myself impressed with Betts, who I'd not read before, and interested in what she could create within the broader scope of a full length novel. She showed off a nice talent for plot creation and pacing, smooth narrative, sensual romance, and heated sexuality that would really shine in a longer-length format.

Reviewed for One Good Book Deserves Another.

reviewText:
"All I Vant For Christmas"
Connor Drake is a millionaire and a vampire with a problem. He wants his family to celebrate an old-fashioned holiday season. But his brother and sister like the thrill of shocking people with the more shocking aspects of being a vampire. When Connor mentions this to a good friend, she suggests he hire a party planner she knows to at least give him the celebration he wants. Jillian Parker has mixed feelings as she heads to an interview to plan a party that could make her name. The timing couldn't be better either because Jillian has just decided to break out of her rut and take more of what life has to offer.

As their meeting goes on, Connor knows that his party might be all he wants for the holidays but what he really wants is Jillian. After Jillian agrees to the job and the unusual conditions, she quickly discovers the problems with this dysfunctional family are interesting to say the least. But she is determined to pull off the best Norman Rockwell Christmas party she can. From the minute they meet the passion buzzing around Connor and Jillian is undeniable and they aren't really fighting it anyway. However, now on to the bigger problem - that old fashion family Christmas party.

Can a special party planner find the key to put a family back together? Jillian just might be able to in "All I Vant For Christmas". The passion that sprang up between Jillian and Connor was all but overwhelming to both of them because it was so unexpected. I loved watching how Connor put Jillian's fear to rest and how their love bloomed. Even more, I enjoyed watching how their feelings were changing the aspects with the entire family. "All I Vant For Christmas" is a fun and erotic journey into an old fashioned Christmas.

"A Vampire in Her Stocking"
Vivian Harrison has been an assistant at the news station for many years. Over these years, she has fallen in love with her boss. However, Vivian hasn't done anything about it because there is one major problem - she is a vampire and he doesn't know it nor does he really like them. Sean Spice is an on air reporter who has found out he has a major illness and is dying. Sean has made arrangement to leave the station but he hasn't told the one person closest to him - his amazing assistant. Now time is up and he has to tell her before he leaves.

Vivian can't believe the news and the fact that Sean is dying. Confiding in her best friend, Vivian is reminded that she can allow Sean to live forever, but Vivian knows Sean would never agree to it. Image her surprise to find a ribbon-wrapped Sean under her tree, even worse, he has been changed into a vampire. Vivian will have to help him come to grips with his new reality and the anger he feels. Knowing she has lost Sean forever, Vivian helps him with the basics and then lets him walk away. Heart broken, Vivian hopes that Sean will find happiness and maybe someday so will she.

"A Vampire in Her Stocking" gives Vivian everything she has always wanted and then has her lose it all. Watching Vivian and Sean brace up to the news that he would be leaving in order to die without public knowledge, hurt. I had to give Vivian points for helping Sean through his anger, while knowing he has lost all hope for love. I could have shook Sean a few times, but still understood the shock he was going through. However, I loved how when I thought all hope was lost, Sean gave Vivian the best Christmas present ever - his heart. "A Vampire in Her Stocking" proves that Christmas joy can come from the deepest of lows and a belief in true love.

"It's A Wonderful Bite"
Angelina Ricci is one woman who knows what she wants and how she wants it. Of course, seeing the evidence of her work in bringing love to two of her good friends warms her heart at Connor's party. Even if it was outside of her dating agency for vampires. Angelina feels the warmth and love of her friends and wants it for herself. Even having her longtime lover with her doesn't ease the want because even after all the years together, they are still just lovers. Ian Hart truly loves Angelina even if he doesn't talk about it. He has always been one of those strong, silent types along with being a cop. After the party, Ian just wants to watch his favorite movie and then have a passionate night with Angelina.

Angelina wakes up after their wonderful night to find herself in a different reality, one in which both she and Ian are human and cops. Not realizing what happened right off, Angelina soon discovers wanting more can give you less. The love that she wants so much again seems to be just out of her reach. In this reality, a stake out bumps them up against vampires and any chance at love is lost to both Angelina and Ian by the end of that night. Shock awakens Angelina to discover Ian right next to her and she has another chance to accept the love that has always been there.

"It's a Wonderful Bite" takes Angelina on a journey to discover that the love she wants and hopes for is right in front of her. I watched as Angelina's envy at her friends' happiness blinded her to what she already had. The real life dream was a shock and heartache that Angelina never expected with Ian. I loved how Ian sprang his Christmas surprise on Angelina and gave her the best Christmas present available. "It's a Wonderful Bite" takes a holiday classic and shows one woman that her life really is a wonderful thing.

The Bite Before Christmas is three great stories showing that love can come in many forms. I loved the fun love between Connor and Jillian that loosened up a dysfunctional family. I wanted to hug Sean and Vivian several times and hoped their love would be discovered in time. I saw Angelina learn love's most important lesson and achieve her heart's desire with Ian. The Bite Before Christmas is a passionate and loving book that shares the joy and love that Christmas can bring - with a paranormal twist.

Jo

As you might expect from the title (and the cover) this is a lighter collection...the tie that binds the three novellas together is a vampire named Angelina.  She meddles (in a good way) in the romantic lives of two other couples--the stories that make up the first two stories.  The first one is the lightest, the second one gets a little more serious as it involves the involuntary changing of a man with a terminal illness.  The third story is one for Angelina herself, and it is the most serious (in an obvious "It's a Wonderful Life" sort of way).

The background for the stories is that it is a given that vampires have been accepted as real, and overall are integrating into society.  There is very little blood lust/blood sucking going on (well, yes, from those Icky Criminals in the third story, but overall it's all very sanitary).

The author did a great job of setting the background in an unobtrusive way, and then just giving us the stories.  If the author was so inclined, she could easily expand into full length novels where we could learn the hows and whys of the world, but really she does a great job giving us just enough that she can stick to the shorter tales, and the shorter tales feel complete.  And naughty.  Did I mention naughty?  These are a little naughty.

Great little set of stories if these are what you are in the mood for.  Recommended!

This book is difficult for me to review.  I see it as both good news and a bad news review.

First the good news: this is a well-written story ... the main characters are clearly defined as the story unfolds; and I totally endorse the Christian values in this book.

The bad probably relates more to my personal reading tastes than to any real issue with this book or its author.  This book deals heavily in the characters' feelings and emotions.  For my personal fiction reading, I strongly prefer action, adventure, intrigue, etc.

That said, if you like to read fiction about relationships and feelings, then this book is for you.  The author did very well with that style of writing.

I usually avoid Christian lit. like the plague but occasionally I get pulled into one from a recommendation from a friend or just from guilt. Usually I'm disappointed.  So starting this book I didn't expect much. The same story- girl has something happen to her, girl struggles, girl meets guy, guy helps her strengthen her faith, they fall in love, everyone rides off into the sunset - seems to happen again and again. Unfortunately this one fit the bill, fortunately it did it fairly well.

The usual scenario played itself out, but between the past chasing the main character and finding out more about the guy, the plot has enough tension to keep me interested. Slogging through the first couple chapters was a bit tedious because it jumps around but I think that the different view points lent well to the story. By the end I was trying to guess how they would all twine together.

The characters were all real, and like able enough, but I don't think I will remember any of them after I've read a few more books. The love story was fairly light, and a bit abrupt at the end, but it also lent to the building tension Morally, most of the book was sound and I don't think most Christians will have too many problems with the theology.

So for my expectations it was a pretty good book. As a book in general it was...okay. If you love Christian literature, you'll probably enjoy this book.
summary: Not Bad Though Not Really Very Different

I love and enjoy Linda Nichols books. This one is the first book of Ms. Nichols that i read. I wish she would write more! very inspiring and moving!

Wonderfully written main character, while I am not overly religious, I still felt that the story help up on it's own merits.  A very well written, story with great pacing.  Also very emotional.  If you were on the fence, like I was, about the religious aspects of the story I would say to give it a try anyway. It does not beat you over the head with it and for that I loved it.

I thought this was a sweet, touching story overall. It is a contemporary Christian fiction book. The characters and plot were interesting and unique. I really felt for all of them. The writing was good and drew me in from the beginning. Some parts were beautiful. The ending was fitting and I liked it. The main theme is forgiveness. Recommended.

this is an interesting, captivating story, read well.  keeps your attention.  Will definitely buy more by the author and the reader.

This book turned out to be a disappointment and a time-waster. I had hoped it wouldn't end up being cliche or forgettable because of the unusual beginning and the direction in which I THOUGHT it was going. But the story turned out to be boring, and I didn't find any of the characters remotely interesting. I had absolutely no sympathy for Samantha (the teenage girl archetype is overdone and tiresome), the character development of Bridget was mediocre, and Alasdair, the male protagonist, had nothing even CLOSE to a personality. As a general rule, if an author wants to go with a theme that's been done several times (such as a prodigal turning back to the faith) it has to be done exceptionally well.

As horrible as it sounds, the list of complaints could go on and on. As a sixteen year old, I feel I could have crafted this story better than Nichols and that's without being presumptuous. All in all, I feel like the book had potential, but it was tragically wasted. I will not be reading any more books by this Christian author. Generally, I enjoy Christian fiction - historical, contemporary, and suspense - but I am selective about what I read. I am not giving this a positive review because I am not satisfied with merely a predictable Christian message and a failed attempt at originality.

Oh my I just finished this book!  It is a modern fiction that could happen anywhere in America!  Our story revolves around a young woman named Mary.  She is caught up in a meth producing operation as their supply buyer.  Our story eventually joins up with a widower pastor who is a work-a-holic.  Alasdair, who's wife died just two years ago has a preteen daughter Samantha, who has numerous issues of her own with her mother dying, and twin toddlers.  Oh my readers of this review, I hate to give any of the books secrets away with much more detail, so I won't!

I myself read a book to escape reality as it is today, and this book was by no means an escape.  Although it was well written, I didn't enjoy reading it as I have other books I have read lately.  The issues are ones that need to be dealt with however.  What can be going through a meth addicts' mind was absolutely frightening!  I was so concerned for the safety of the characters in this book!  Alasdair's overworking was the classic example of doing the work of God, but not having that flair that you have when you commune with Him.  Alasdair is spread so thin, that all of his life suffers, and not just his, his family as well.  All in all, it was a good book, with a true to life story line.

I would like to thank Bethany House for the opportunity to review their books and for the free copy that I received.

Mary Bridget is a lost soul to say the least. She knows the steps she took to end up in a dingy trailer with an unstable housemate and a boyfriend that has lost his mind to the meth they cook. Mary is a runner to the drug stores by day and terrified in her own self-induced prison by night. That is until a small voice she hadn't listened to in years tells her to run away. In a more deceivingly idyllic part of the world, Reverend Alasdair MacPherson is drowning. His family is struggling to keep it together, he has no time for his children, let alone his writing, radio show, appearances, or the church that started it all. His overbearing sisters have been picking up the slack over the past two years since his wife died, but even they are slowing losing control. The family needs help and no one seems to be able to step up and take control. Mary Bridget and Alasdair are both on a collision course for disaster, and it would seem that all both need is each other. But can Alasdair wake up in time to see what he has found in Mary, and can Mary keep him despite her past, which races to catch up every day?
 This novel is haunting, simply grabbing the reader from the first sentence and doesn't let go until the end. The plot is made up of a series of chance crossings and coincidence, leading up to a twist at the end of the novel that sent chills down my spine. What I think has made this novel so unforgettable lies not in the plot itself, but in the characters. Even in Mary's worse moments, as the worst person that she can be, I found myself not just sympathetic to her but heart-broken for her. Her fear was clear and tangible. Her situation is unapologetic, making it all the more triumphant when it seems that she left it behind. This goes for all the characters, my heart hurt for Samantha and the twins. My frustration with Alasdair was overruled by the pity felt for his situation. Even the often proclaimed "battle-ax" Winifred has the opportunity for sympathy The characters and story are built upon layers of depth, often jumping from the perspective of Mary, to the 13 year old speech and slang of Samantha, to the skeevy and desperate thoughts of Bob, to the frightening thoughts of Jonah high on meth. There is a lot of Biblical verse, and more than I normally "tolerate" for a 5 star novel. However, Nichols was able to incorporate the words so beautifully, that even when directly quoted, it never felt cheesy of overdone.
 This novel is definitely worth picking up and adding to your personal library. Nichols is triumphant in writing a novel that appeals on so many levels, not only successfully, but fully. I was completely satisfied with it as an adventure, as a drama, a cautionary tale, as a romance, and the list goes on. Linda Nichols is an author to keep an eye on and this particular novel will stay with me for a long time.

Have you ever wished you could run away from your past?  Have you wanted to hide out and just pray that it never finds you?  Mary Bridget Washburn  needed desperately to get out of the life she was currently living, but can you really reinvent yourself when you're on the wrong side of the law?  Once given the opportunity, will she be brave enough to take it and do what must be done?  Can God really use someone with her past to heal the hurts of a family in crisis?

Not too far away is a father who is caught between secrets from his past and a congregation that is divided in whether he should be their pastor; a daughter at the beginning of her teen years, who is scared and desperately wants someone, anyone to show they care; and twin babies who just need someone to love and care for them.

This book is a powerful reminder of the power of intercessory prayer, God's grace and mercy, and the way God can use his people if we'll just get out of His way.  Linda Nichols seamlessly weaves all these truths throughout this book.  You will find your heart racing as Mary runs for her life, pray with the intercessors when Satan is trying his best to wreak havoc in different situations, cry when they cry, and laugh when they laugh.

Not a Sparrow Falls will warm your heart in many ways, and leave you wanting more.

This book was provided to me by Bethany House Book Reviewers.

Linda Nichols is a powerful writer, and the Lord never fails to perfectly time the entrance into my heart and life.  Bethany House repackaged Not a Sparrow Falls earlier this year, and the book has sat patiently waiting to be read. Well, what I found between its pages was God's gentle reminder, and here I quote my husband's frequent advice, "Don't be quick to judge someone, because you never know what God is doing in their life."

This book is filled with flawed characters. There is a preacher, Alasdair, who has been blindsided by tragedy. His family suffers greatly because of his neglect, and he doesn't even realize the state of affairs. Then you have Mary Washburn, a woman who has allowed her life to become trapped into the nightmare of drug addiction and manufacturing. Neither one of these poor souls really has a clue what to do about their circumstance, but both of them are desperate...desperate for change.

God begins to lay the burden of prayer upon the hearts of His prayer warriors, and things begin to change - slowly and subtly. Mary finds herself in circumstances she never dreamed of, and Alasdair finds his home life taking turns for the better, while his pastorship of the local church begins a downward spiral. Where these two lives intersect, grace abounds, and mercy never ceases. The end result is something only God could do.

I've been privileged to see lives transformed from hopelessness. While some would find this plot line a bit far fetched, I find it quite believable and full of an encouragement infused by the promises of God. Linda Nichols understands God's tender care for the "least of these", and her stories encourage others to be aware of His leadership in their lives, and not to be afraid to follow.

This really is an amazing story. I have loved every story I've ever read by Linda Nichols, and I hope it won't be long until I'm privileged to read another.
summary: A touching story about God's grace...

reviewText: Written in 2002, Not a Sparrow Falls  was a 2003 Christy Awards finalist in the Contemporary category. Nichols handles difficult topics to write about within Christian fiction with grace and confidence. The message of redemption through Christ is seen in the pages of the book.

This was a very good book and I enjoyed reading it.  It's a lot about relationships, past and present, but mostly to me it's about redemption.  About how we can know God and fall away, but He's always ready to forgive and take us back.  My favorite line in the whole book is:  "You can't out-sin the cross."  That is so true!  Thank you, Lord!  I highly recommend this book.

When I first began reading this book, I was a bit hesitant about reading it because it does not fall into the categories of books that I prefer to read. What propelled me to keep reading was my curiousity about the grandmother of the main character, as well as how the plot seemed to sort of verge to the right of what I tried to predict would happen next as I read. I enjoy reading books that are not completely predictable, but not so unpredictable that the events are absurd. This would definitely fall under that heading.
With this book, I got a peak into a lifestyle (of drugs) that I have blessedly never experienced first hand, and it opened my eyes to the desperation and hopelessness that accompanies it. I also got a look into the polar opposite of that lifestyle - that of a pastor and the politics within a specific denomination. Along with these two heavy topics, Nichols also seamlessly weaves the equally heavy topics of depression and suicide beautifully, albeit bittersweetly. I found myself shedding tears over the book, not once, but twice. The wisdom addressing these topics was right on target and fit very naturally into the plot without the book coming across as "preachy." Each of the characters, no matter how small his or her part in the plot, was well-defined and unique, and I appreciated each one. All of the "loose ends" were accounted for and tied up, and every character seemed to reach a place of redemption in their own way.
This book was very satisfying and I am glad I decided to read it.

Many of the books I have read of late deal with the subject of forgiveness - particularly of self (is God trying to get through this thick head?!). The latest book I have read with this important topic as a main theme is `Not a Sparrow Falls' by Linda Nichols.

Here is the synopsis of this novel:

Two Desperate People - One with All the Answers ...One with None
Mary Bridget Washburn is tired of running, tired of being haunted by the empty shell her life has become. How in the world did the little girl she once was become a woman on the wrong side of the law?
Determined to make a new start, she escapes to the quaint city of Alexandria, Virginia, where she takes on her mother's identity and finds sanctuary in the shadow of a decades-old church. But the little girl's plea proves to be her undoing, and the reverend...well, someone's got to open his eyes before disaster comes calling.
Can Mary Bridget and her tainted past stay hidden long enough for her to bring hope to a family falling apart?

Here is the biography of the author:

Linda Nichols ([...]) is a graduate of the University of Washington, is an award-winning and bestselling novelist with a unique gift for touching readers' hearts with her stories. Not A Sparrow Falls, her bestselling debut novel for the Christian fiction market, was a 2003 Christy Awards finalist in the Contemporary category. She and her family make their home in Tacoma, Washington.

The main character in this novel is Mary Bridget Washburn, age 25, who, at the beginning of the story, was in her own personal prison as the girlfriend of Jonah, her childhood friend who had turned into a crystal meth addict/supplier; she was his accomplice in his `business.' She'd grown up in a Christian home, so was well aware that this lifestyle was not what God had in mind for her. At her earliest opportunity, she fled the scene, and took on the identity of her deceased mother, Bridget Collins.

In Alexandria, Virginia, she was hired at a grocery store as a cashier. She made the acquaintance of three sisters -Lorna, Winifred, and Fiona. Lorna invited her to the home of their brother, Alasdair MacPherson, a Presbyterian pastor who was pasturing the church that had been led by his father before him.
Alasdair was a widower; his wife had died two years prior, leaving him with days-old twins, Cameron and Bonnie, and an eleven year old daughter, Samantha. He was more interested in his work then in his family, and was still grieving the loss of Anna.

Circumstances conspired, and Mary/Bridget - now known as Bridie - was hired as the nanny for the children. Seeing the pain and neglect that had been visited upon the children, Bridie, as a form of penance and in love, transformed this family.

God tells Bridie that He has an assignment for her:

She scraped and scrubbed and there, in the gray dishwater, without wanting to, she saw the vision again - Alasdair, his face open and smiling, Samantha laughing, the twins loved and cared for. She turned the hot water on full blast as if to wash it away. This is what I'm going to do, she thought she'd heard. And you may help. (p. 132)

Throughout this book, both Bridie and Alasdair were relentlessly pursued by God. Bridie's maternal grandmother, Hattie, never stopped praying for her, and never gave up hope that the Lord would bring Bridie home.

As Bridie is making this new life for herself, she is tormented by the choices she had made in her past, and is still imprisoned - never knowing if she will be pursued for her crimes. She is forever looking over her shoulder. Despite that, she remembers the truths of Scripture that she had memorized as a little girl.

I loved this insight shared with Alasdair by his former seminary professor, Professor Cuthbert. Professor Cuthbert perfectly describes what can happen to people who study in seminary and/or get into full-time ministry:

..."But I'll be the first to acknowledge that my faith has been somewhat top-heavy. North of the neck, shall we say?" (p. 187)

He went on to explain what happened when he had won a fight over his pulpit:

"The building was mine. The congregation was mine. Newby left. Took some members with him, but we were basically unscathed. The only problem was, the hand of the Lord seemed to have stopped moving among us. He'd set us aside. And I knew why. I'd forgotten what I was about, why I was left here on earth. I'd gotten my calling confused with my job." He gazed at Alasdair's face, but Alasdair knew he was seeing the past. "I kept on preaching, but it was no good. After a year or so I took the job at the seminary. The church carried on with someone else. You see," he finished, a bittersweet smile on his lips, "I'd forgotten who was the real captain of the ship. The church wasn't mine, but His." (p. 189)

They continued their discussion with this sage piece of advice from Professor Cuthbert:

"You know, Alasdair, the older I get, the more I realize only one thing matters."
"What is that?"
"To know Him. To walk with Him. Just as Adam did in the garden in the cool of the day. There's nothing else." (p. 190)

I really loved 'Not a Sparrow Falls'! The message in this book is that God is a God of second (and third and fourth, etc...) chances, and that His main objective is for us to know Him. And no matter what we think of ourselves, He is always in love with us and never stops pursuing us. That is a message that needs to be repeated over and over again, and Mrs. Nichols does it with such love and grace! I loved how this story showed many times over - in the examples of Bridie and in her grandma Hattie - that God uses us for His purposes, and we have the privilege to be a part of His Kingdom work!

I loved the ending of the story, and hope that Mrs. Nichols might someday continue the story of the MacPherson family.

This book was provided by Bethany House Publishing for review purposes.
